items.title: Dave Liebman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The point of the psychological aspect of being so enamored by Trane and so into it and having to deal with Coltrane my whole life, musically

ctx.x: It’s whatever you want it to be.

The point of the psychological aspect of being so enamored by Trane and so into it and having to deal with Coltrane my whole life, musically, that I’m not going to be Trane, that in fact I may not even be the left pinkie of his, and that I haven’t heard anything better and never did and never will, blah blah blah blah blah blah, etc., etc. By now, in the early ’80s, this is a fact of life. I already had – I won’t say I coped with it, but I had found I’m not. I admitted it. I admit it. I’m not. This sounds all…

I tell my students, you’re learning to be a jazz musician, and that involves learning to be an improviser. One of the things you have to learn is how to improvise as a career. That’s what we all do. Did you ever read a book called The Third Wave, by Alvin Toffler?
